questions.q: In one line, what is a Wedge Drop?
choices: A close down through the averages
A close under the 200-day line
A retest of the averages after a drop
A close up through the averages
questions.answer: A close down through the averages
questions.why: A close down through the averages. TraderLion: the Wedge Drop happens when the market trades back below the moving averages after a strong rally. Kell: the drop is price falling through the averages with an influx of sellers. Deepvue says sellers push the stock below key averages. The 200-day is a separate gate for shorts.
questions.lesson_line: A rally, a rest on the averages, then the close through them. That is the drop.

wrong.A close under the 200-day line: The 200-day is the gate for a short. The drop is the close down through the averages the stock rested on.
wrong.A close up through the averages: That is the mirror, the Wedge Pop: a close up through the averages from under them. The drop closes down through them.
wrong.A retest of the averages after a drop: That is the downside EMA Crossback, a retest met with resistance after the drop. The drop is the close down through the averages.

questions.simple: A Wedge Drop is a close back down through the moving averages after a rally and a short rest.

reasons: fixed before (cold check)

questions.q: For us a Wedge Drop above the 200-day is a sell signal for a long, never a short.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. Above the 200-day, a Wedge Drop is only a sell signal for a long. We short only below the 200-day simple moving average, unless it is a parabolic short, which is a different setup. Below the 200-day it is a short only if the other gates also pass.
questions.lesson_line: Above the 200-day it tells you to sell. Below it, and only below it, it can be shorted.
questions.simple: True. Above the 200-day, a Wedge Drop only tells a long holder to sell, and we never short it there.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (B26, a hard rule)

questions.q: In Kell's cycle, what comes right before the Wedge Drop?
choices: An extension, then a tight stall
A base of many months, then a pop
A steady slide with no pause
A gap up out of a flat base
questions.answer: An extension, then a tight stall
questions.why: An extension, then a tight stall. After an Exhaustion Extension, prices often trade in a tight range as the averages catch up. Kell: price trades tight into the moving averages as there are fewer new buyers. A big extension is not always there: sometimes the price only trades sideways and loses momentum. It does not come out of a base of months or a steady slide.
questions.lesson_line: The top, then the rest on the averages, then the drop. Learn the order.

wrong.A base of many months, then a pop: That is a base for a long. The stall before a drop is days, not months.
wrong.A steady slide with no pause: After the extension price rests in a tight range while the averages catch up. The drop follows a rest, not a slide.
wrong.A gap up out of a flat base: That is a breakout. The drop follows a top, not a breakout.

questions.simple: First a rally stretches out, then price rests tight on its averages for a few days. The drop comes after that.

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: No short more than ___% under the trigger level.
questions.why: 4%. We never short more than 4% under the trigger level. It mirrors our no-chase line for longs, 4% past the buy point, because shorts are our long setups reversed. Past 4%, we skip the trade.
questions.lesson_line: Four percent under the trigger and I am done. I would rather miss it than chase it.
questions.simple: The limit is 4%. If the price is already more than 4% under the trigger level, we skip the short.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (C28, mirrored by D47)

questions.q: Once a Wedge Drop short is closed out, one new close under both averages is enough for a second short.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. A second short needs a new stall and a new close under both averages. The drop is a one-day event that the next day confirms or cancels. Like any re-entry, it is a new trade with its own stop and every rule.
questions.lesson_line: The drop is a one-day event. Once it fails, the next short needs a new setup.
questions.simple: False. A second short needs a new stall as well as a new close under both averages.

reasons: rests on a proposed card criterion awaiting owner review

questions.q: Where does the stop go on a Wedge Drop short, by our default?
choices: A few cents over the trigger day's high
A few cents under the day's low
A few cents over the 200-day line
Exactly on the trigger day's high
questions.answer: A few cents over the trigger day's high
questions.why: A few cents over the trigger day's high. Stop first. A short loses when price rises, so the stop sits above the entry. The high of the day is the main stop, the mirror of the low of day on a long. It goes a few cents past the high, not exactly on it. TraderLion also puts it just above the recent high. The card also allows a few cents over the higher of the trigger day and the day before. We prefer stops 1 to 3% away, and up to 5% is acceptable. Past 5%, we mostly wait for a tighter trigger.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first: a few cents over the trigger day's high, not exactly on it.

wrong.A few cents under the day's low: That is the long's stop, mirrored the wrong way. A short's risk is above the entry.
wrong.A few cents over the 200-day line: The 200-day is the gate for taking the short, not the place for its stop. The stop goes over the trigger day's high.
wrong.Exactly on the trigger day's high: Our rule is a few cents past the day's extreme, not exactly on it.

questions.simple: A short loses when the price rises, so the stop goes a few cents over the trigger day's high.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook and a held decision (D-008, where the stop goes)

questions.q: On our card the stall runs 3 to 10 sessions between the top and the trigger day.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. The card says the stall runs 3 to 10 sessions between the top and the trigger day. Those numbers are the card's, not Kell's. He only says that after the extension, price trades tight into the moving averages as there are fewer new buyers.
questions.lesson_line: Three to ten days of rest on the averages. Then the close decides.
questions.simple: True. Our card gives the stall three to ten sessions between the top and the trigger day.

reasons: rests on a proposed card number

questions.q: The index itself forms a Wedge Drop. What is that a warning of?
choices: The whole market is weakening
Only a few big stocks are tired
A pause before the next leg up
A buy point for the market leaders
questions.answer: The whole market is weakening
questions.why: The market as a whole is weakening. TraderLion: when an index like the S&P 500 or Nasdaq forms a Wedge Drop, it is a warning. Several leaders in Wedge Drops is a sign to get defensive. Bracco read the Nasdaq's drop as the start of another leg down.
questions.lesson_line: An index Wedge Drop is a warning for the whole market, not just one stock.

wrong.A buy point for the market leaders: Several leaders in Wedge Drops is a sign to get defensive, not to buy.
wrong.Only a few big stocks are tired: TraderLion: an index Wedge Drop warns that the market as a whole is weakening, not a few names.
wrong.A pause before the next leg up: Bracco read the Nasdaq's drop as the start of another leg down. Kell read an index drop as confirmation of a deeper pullback.

questions.simple: A Wedge Drop in the index warns that the whole market is getting weaker, not just one stock.

deeper.example: Kell dated this on QQQ: an Exhaustion Extension on 2/2, a Wedge Drop on 2/16 and 2/17, an EMA Crossback on 2/23. That index drop sat above the 200-day, so for us it was a sell signal for longs, not a short.

reasons: a card rule, proposed

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: A short still under 1R of profit after ___ sessions is covered.
questions.why: 10. A trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is closed, which frees the money. For a short, closed means covered.
questions.lesson_line: Ten days and nothing. The money has somewhere better to be.
questions.simple: After 10 trading days with less than 1R of profit, we cover the short and free the money for something better.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (C33, the time stop)

questions.q: Before the trigger day, how many of the last 10 closes must sit above the 20-day EMA on our card?
choices: At least 5
At least 7
At least 8
At least 9
questions.answer: At least 8
questions.why: At least 8 of the 10. The card wants at least 8 of the 10 closes before the trigger day above the 20-day EMA. That is the prior bounce. For a short, Kell drew it as a fast rally in a bear market. It puts in a lower high and then drops. A dip under the 20-day is allowed, so it does not need all 10. The 8 is the card's proposed number.
questions.lesson_line: No bounce, no drop. Eight of the last ten closes over the 20-day EMA is the bounce.

wrong.At least 5: Five of ten is only half the closes. The card wants eight.
wrong.At least 7: Seven of ten falls short. The card wants eight.
wrong.At least 9: Nine is stricter than the card. A dip under the 20-day is allowed, and eight of ten is the line.

questions.simple: At least 8 of the last 10 closes must sit above the 20-day average. That is what makes it a bounce.

reasons: rests on a proposed card number
tied to a held decision (D-021)

questions.story: The stock has an RS rating of 92 and leads its group. It stalls four days on its averages, then closes under them, under the 200-day.
questions.q: Short it?
choices: No; a leader, not the weakest
Yes; it closed under the averages
Yes; RS does not matter on shorts
questions.answer: No; a leader, not the weakest
questions.why: No. Shorts are the mirror: the weakest stocks, an RS rating of 20 or less, in the weakest groups. A leader with strong RS is the B- row, and TraderLion says to avoid strong uptrending stocks.
questions.lesson_line: Short the weakest, not the strongest. A leader that lost its averages once is not weak.

wrong.Yes; it closed under the averages: The close is one gate. The RS rule is another, and a 92 fails it.
wrong.Yes; RS does not matter on shorts: It matters in mirror image: 20 or less, in a weak group.

questions.q: A Wedge Drop short in a $6 stock trading $3 million a day is fine if the chart is clean.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. We trade only stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day. This stock fails both tests, at $6 and $3 million. A clean chart does not fix that.
questions.lesson_line: Price and liquidity come before the chart. Under $10 or under $20 million a day, pass.
questions.simple: False. We trade only stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day, so this one fails twice.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (B23)

questions.q: You hold a long and did not sell the second extension. By Kell's deck, what takes you out?
choices: The Wedge Drop signal
The EMA Crossback retest
The Wedge Pop breakout
A close under the 200-day
questions.answer: The Wedge Drop signal
questions.why: The Wedge Drop. Kell: if you did not sell the second extension, the wedge drop should take you out of the trade. TraderLion agrees: use it as a signal to protect profits and reduce exposure. Our card calls it the last exit, and holding a long through it is a named mistake. A drop reclaimed within a few sessions was only a shakeout. Buy again on a new setup.
questions.lesson_line: The drop is the last exit for a long. Not a reason to hope.

wrong.The EMA Crossback retest: The crossback comes after the drop. Kell: ideally any long positions have been closed at the Wedge Drop.
wrong.The Wedge Pop breakout: A pop is a close up through the averages, the mirror setup. It is a buy setup, not an exit.
wrong.A close under the 200-day: Kell names the drop as the backstop. The 200-day is where longs stop being allowed, not his exit signal.

questions.simple: The Wedge Drop. It is the last exit for a long holder, so you sell when it comes.

questions.q: No new Wedge Drop short in the 3 sessions before an earnings report.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. We take no new trades in the 3 days before a report, and the card counts them as sessions. A short you already hold stays through a report only if it is up 5R.
questions.lesson_line: No new short in the 3 sessions before a report.
questions.simple: True. We open no new short in the 3 sessions before an earnings report.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (B22)

questions.q: In the stall, how far may a close sit from the 9 EMA on our card?
choices: No more than 0.5 ATR
No more than 1 ATR
No more than 2 ATR
No more than 5%
questions.answer: No more than 1 ATR
questions.why: No more than 1 ATR. Through the stall no close is more than 1 ATR from the 9 EMA. ATR is the stock's own usual daily range, so the test fits each stock. Kell: price trades tight into the moving averages. The 1 ATR is the card's proposed number.
questions.lesson_line: The stall hugs the 9 EMA. Far from it is not a stall.

wrong.No more than 5%: The stall test is set in ATR, the stock's own usual daily range, not in a fixed percent.
wrong.No more than 0.5 ATR: That is stricter than the card. The line is 1 ATR.
wrong.No more than 2 ATR: Too loose. The card's line is 1 ATR from the 9 EMA.

questions.simple: No close in the stall sits more than one typical day's range away from the 9 EMA.

reasons: rests on a proposed card number
tied to a held decision (D-021)

questions.story: In a downtrend the stock bounces into its falling 50-day and turns down, under the high of the last 60 sessions. Then it stalls four days.
questions.q: What kind of top is that?
choices: A lower high, the bear-market form
An extension top over the 20-day
A failed push past the prior day's high
No top yet; it is only a pause
questions.answer: A lower high, the bear-market form
questions.why: A lower high. The bounce peaks under the highest high of the 60 sessions before it. Kell's bear-market diagram: a fast rally puts in a lower high, then drops. Our own shorts are often a decent pop back up, rejected at the 50-day or 20-day EMA, below the 200-day. The card accepts three tops: an extension, a lower high, or a failed push past the prior day's high.
questions.lesson_line: A pop into the falling 50-day that fails is the picture we want.

wrong.An extension top over the 20-day: An extension is a close far above the 20-day EMA. This bounce died at a falling average.
wrong.A failed push past the prior day's high: That is a day that fails to clear the prior day's high. This bounce peaked under the high of the last 60 sessions.
wrong.No top yet; it is only a pause: A bounce that turns under the prior high and stalls is the top. The drop then confirms it.

questions.simple: The bounce peaked under the highest high of the last 60 sessions, which makes it a lower high.

deeper.example: GS in August 2011 was this picture. The bounce died at the falling 50-day, a four-day stall followed, and the whole move followed the averages down. The short came on the close under both averages at 131.23.

reasons: rests on a proposed card criterion awaiting owner review

questions.q: A stall that makes a new high in its last 3 sessions is still a valid Wedge Drop setup.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. The card wants no new high in the last 3 sessions of the stall. A new high there ends the setup before the trigger. A stall that is still making highs has not rested, so the averages have not caught up to price. Wait for quiet days and a fresh stall.
questions.lesson_line: A stall that keeps making highs is not stalling. Wait for the quiet days.
questions.simple: False. If the stall makes a new high in its last 3 sessions, it is not resting and the setup is off.

reasons: rests on a proposed card criterion awaiting owner review

questions.story: The trigger day gaps down and opens 12% under its 9 EMA. The stall and the averages all checked out.
questions.q: Short at the open, or pass?
choices: Pass; over 10% under the 9 EMA
Pass; the stall was too short
Short; gap confirms the top
Short at half size, same stop
questions.answer: Pass; over 10% under the 9 EMA
questions.why: Pass. We skip a short more than 10% under its 9 EMA, checked at the open on a gap down. This one opens 12% under, so it fails, even with the stall and averages in order. The long rule is 10% above the 9 EMA. The short is its mirror.
questions.lesson_line: A drop that is already stretched is a chase with a different name.

wrong.Pass; the stall was too short: The story says the stall checked out. The reason to pass is the stretch under the 9 EMA.
wrong.Short; gap confirms the top: A gap down can look like confirmation. The rule checks the stretch at the open, and it says skip.
wrong.Short at half size, same stop: Size does not fix a stretched entry. The rule is skip.

questions.simple: Pass. The open is more than 10% under the 9 EMA, so the drop is already stretched and we skip it.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (C29, mirrored by D47)

questions.q: When does the first cover usually come on a Wedge Drop short?
choices: Day 3 at the earliest, or later
Day 1, to lock in a quick gain
At exactly 3R, whatever the day
Never; hold it all to the end
questions.answer: Day 3 at the earliest, or later
questions.why: Day 3 at the earliest, and often later. The first cover is a judgment, not a fixed third at 3R. We very rarely sell on day 1 of the buy. Selling into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, or at about 5 to 10R, is often best. A short is a long setup reversed, so the same holds.
questions.lesson_line: Rarely cover on day 1. Day 3 at the earliest, often into a longer move.

wrong.Day 1, to lock in a quick gain: We very rarely sell on day 1 of the buy. We usually wait until day 3 at the earliest.
wrong.At exactly 3R, whatever the day: The first sell is a judgment, not a fixed third at 3R.
wrong.Never; hold it all to the end: We do cover. The first cover is a judgment, often into a 3, 5 or 7 day move.

questions.simple: We rarely cover on day 1. We usually wait until day 3 at the earliest, often into a longer move.

reasons: rests on the owner's ruling D-013 (the first sell is a judgment)
the short side mirrors the long side (D47)

questions.q: Short at 55.16 with the stop at 56.28. How far above the fill is the stop, in percent?
questions.why: 2.03%. The stop minus the fill, over the fill: (56.28 - 55.16) / 55.16 x 100 = 2.03%. That fits inside the 3% a stop usually sits within, and it is a loss on the position, not the account. It was WHR's stop in August 2002.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first, distance second, size last. Measure the distance before the size.
questions.simple: The stop is 2.03% above the fill. That is the gap between them divided by the fill, and it fits inside 3%.

reasons: +2 a computed key
+1 fixed before

wrong.1.12%: Used the dollar gap as if it were the percent.
wrong.20.3%: A decimal slip, one place too far right.
wrong.98.0%: Gave the fill as a share of the stop, not the gap between them.

questions.story: You shorted the close under both averages at 50.00, stop 51.20. Two days later it closes back above both averages. Your stop has not been hit.
questions.q: On our card, what now?
choices: Cover; the reclaim is the exit
Hold; your stop is still above it
Add; it is now a better price
Move the stop to breakeven
questions.answer: Cover; the reclaim is the exit
questions.why: Cover. TraderLion: if the stock regains its moving averages and pushes higher, exit the short. Our card says a close back above both averages is the cover. HPQ did this on day 2 and its stop was hit that same day. The slide came in July, without the trade. A second short needs a new stall and a new close under both.
questions.lesson_line: The reclaim cancels the drop. Cover, and wait for a new stall.

wrong.Hold; your stop is still above it: The stop is the last line. On our card the reclaim is the setup's own exit, and it came first.
wrong.Add; it is now a better price: Full size at one price with one stop. A reclaimed drop is a cancelled setup, not a second entry.
wrong.Move the stop to breakeven: Breakeven comes between 2R and 5R, once the trade has paid. A reclaim says cover, not trail.

questions.simple: Cover the short. A close back above both averages cancels the drop, so you exit and wait for a new stall.

reasons: rests on a proposed card criterion awaiting owner review
fixed before (cold check)

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: Cover the last third on a close back above the 10-day EMA for a fast mover, the ___-day for a steadier one.
questions.why: 21. Our default trail is the 10-day average for fast movers and the 21-day for steadier ones. We cover the last third on a close back above it, not on a touch. Kell expects a retest of the averages after the drop to meet resistance.
questions.lesson_line: Trail the falling average. Cover the close back above it, not the touch.
questions.simple: The steadier movers use the 21-day average. We cover the last third on a close back above it.

deeper.trap: A rally that stalls under the falling averages is a place to hold, not to panic. The trail covers only on a close back above the 10-day or 21-day. A poke above it that fades by the close is not a cover.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (E52)

questions.q: Shorted at 45.96 with the stop at 46.89. Where is 3R?
questions.why: $43.17. One R is the stop minus the fill: 46.89 - 45.96. Three R below the fill is 45.96 - 3 x (46.89 - 45.96) = 43.17. It is a measuring stick, not a cover order. PCG reached 3R on day 10.
questions.lesson_line: Know your 3R before the open. It is a yardstick, not a cover order.
questions.simple: 3R is the fill minus three times the stop distance, so 43.17. It is a measuring stick, not a cover order.

reasons: a computed key
the first cover is the owner's D-013 judgment, not a fixed 3R cover

wrong.$48.75: Added the 3R to the fill. On a short, 3R is below the fill.
wrong.$44.10: Counted 3R down from the stop, which is only two R below the fill.
wrong.$45.03: Went down one R, not three.

questions.story: A textbook stall breaks under both averages in a stock under its 200-day. The index is in an uptrend and our reading is Green.
questions.q: What is your call?
choices: No short; Green is for longs
Buy the dip; the market is Green
Short; the stock is under its 200
Short, but at half size only
questions.answer: No short; Green is for longs
questions.why: No short. Green is full risk for longs, and the card marks a Green or Yellow reading as a no-trade row for this short. In a Red market we hold mostly cash plus shorts below the 200-day. Being under the 200-day is one gate, not the only one. For a long holder this is still a sell signal.
questions.lesson_line: Read the market before the stock. A short in a Green market is a fight you picked.

wrong.Short; the stock is under its 200: The 200-day is the stock's gate. The market reading is another, and Green fails it.
wrong.Buy the dip; the market is Green: No longs below the 200-day, and a Wedge Drop tells a long holder to sell.
wrong.Short, but at half size only: Size does not fix the market. The card's no-trade row covers the short at any size.

questions.simple: No short. Green is for longs, and the card marks a Green or Yellow reading as a no-trade row for this short.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook and a held decision (D-023, the market filter)
+1 fixed before

questions.story: The stock closes under both averages after a clean stall. But the close sits at 56% of the day's range, mid-bar.
questions.q: Is that the trigger?
choices: No; it must close in the lower 40%
Yes; any close under both averages works
Yes, if volume was heavy that day
No; it must close at the day's low
questions.answer: No; it must close in the lower 40%
questions.why: No. The trigger day closes in the lower 40% of its range. This one closed at 56%. A mid-range close under the averages is undecided, so wait for the next close. LOW 2007-09-07 closed at 56% and was a near miss.
questions.lesson_line: Where the day closes is the vote. Mid-range is no vote.

wrong.Yes; any close under both averages works: A close under both is the event, not the whole trigger. The day must also close in the lower 40% of its range.
wrong.Yes, if volume was heavy that day: Volume is not the test here. Where the day closes in its range is.
wrong.No; it must close at the day's low: The card asks for the lower 40% of the range, not the exact low. A close near the low counts.

questions.simple: No. The day has to close in the lower 40% of its range, and a close near the middle has not decided anything.

deeper.counter: The card does not say a mid-range close can never work. It says the vote is not in yet. In one case, LOW closed at 56% of its range, and it stayed a near miss.

reasons: rests on a proposed card criterion awaiting owner review
fixed before (cold check)

questions.q: In the stall, what does our card want from the volume?
choices: Up days lighter than down days
Up days heavier than down days
Up and down days on equal volume
Volume rising on every day
questions.answer: Up days lighter than down days
questions.why: Up days lighter than down days. The card wants the up days in the stall on lighter volume than the down days. Kell: price trades tight into the moving averages as there are now fewer new buyers.
questions.lesson_line: Quiet up days, heavier down days. Fewer new buyers while price rests on the averages.

wrong.Up days heavier than down days: That is buyers stepping in, not fading. The card wants the up days lighter.
wrong.Up and down days on equal volume: The card wants the up days lighter than the down days, not equal.
wrong.Volume rising on every day: The stall wants quiet up days. Rising volume every day is not a rest.

questions.simple: In a stall, up days trade on lighter volume than down days. That fits fewer new buyers.

reasons: rests on a proposed card criterion awaiting owner review

questions.q: Shorted at 78.94, stop 80.77. The stock trades down to 69.79. How many R is that?
questions.why: 5.0R. One R is the stop minus the fill: 80.77 - 78.94. The gain is the fill minus the price: 78.94 - 69.79. Gain over R: (78.94 - 69.79) / (80.77 - 78.94) = 5.0. That is a measure, not a fixed cover price. EXP reached 3R in three sessions on the way.
questions.lesson_line: Count a short in R too. The gain divided by one R is the R.
questions.simple: The fall from the fill is 5.0 times the stop distance, so it is 5.0R.

reasons: a computed key
when to cover is the owner's D-013 judgment

wrong.0.2R: Flipped the division: one R over the gain.
wrong.0.1R: Divided the gain by the price, not by R.
wrong.1.8R: That is one R in dollars read as R. Divide the gain by it.

questions.story: You are short from 36.65 with the stop at 37.22. It gaps up and opens at 37.40. The first 30-minute bar runs from 37.05 to 37.55.
questions.q: Where is the stop now?
choices: 37.55, the first 30-minute high
37.05, the first 30-minute low
37.40, the price at the open
Cover; the gap is past 2R
questions.answer: 37.55, the first 30-minute high
questions.why: 37.55. A gap through the stop hands it to the first 30 minutes of that day. For a short, the high of the first 30-minute bar becomes the new stop. This is the one exception to never moving a stop wider. The ceiling is 2R: if the first 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, you get out. Here it has not.
questions.lesson_line: A gap through the stop is the one exception. The first 30 minutes decide.

wrong.Cover; the gap is past 2R: The ceiling is 2R. The loss at the 37.55 high is still under it, so it has not been hit.
wrong.37.05, the first 30-minute low: That is the long's rule, mirrored the wrong way. A short's risk is above, so the high is the stop.
wrong.37.40, the price at the open: The gap rule gives the decision to the first 30 minutes. The open is not the stop.

questions.simple: The gap hands the stop to the first 30-minute bar, so the new stop is its high, 37.55.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (B20, mirrored for a short)

questions.q: At the rally back into the falling averages you may add to the short, since Kell's page says so.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. Kell's page does offer the EMA Crossback as a place to add to a short started at the Wedge Drop. Our rule is full size at one price with one stop, and no adding. The crossback can only be its own new trade with its own stop.
questions.lesson_line: One price, one stop. The crossback is a new trade or nothing.
questions.simple: False. Kell's page allows an add, but our rule is one price, one stop, and no adding.

deeper.counter: Kell says the crossback gives a clear area to set a stop against. We take that as the stop for a new trade, sized from that stop. It is not a place to add to the old one.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (A5, over a web view)

questions.story: At 3:50 pm the stock sits well under both averages, near its low of the day. The stall checked out.
questions.q: How do you enter?
choices: Market order now, or next open
A limit order well above the market
Wait three days, then short
Short in the after-hours session
questions.answer: Market order now, or next open
questions.why: Market order now, or at the next open. Our entries are market orders. The card says to place it in the last 15 minutes once the close is clear, or at the next open. We take no new entries outside regular trading hours.
questions.lesson_line: Let the close decide, then enter at market. No limit entries, no after-hours.

wrong.Short in the after-hours session: No new entries outside regular trading hours.
wrong.A limit order well above the market: A limit above the market may never fill on the day that matters. Entries are market orders.
wrong.Wait three days, then short: The trigger is the daily close. Waiting gives away the drop.

questions.simple: Use a market order now, in the last 15 minutes, or at the next open. We enter at market and never after hours.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (E57 and E58)

questions.story: A clean five-day stall breaks under both averages on Monday. The company reports after the close on Tuesday.
questions.q: Short it?
choices: No; a report inside 3 sessions
No; the stall is too short
Yes, at half the usual size
Yes, but cover before the report
questions.answer: No; a report inside 3 sessions
questions.why: No. We take no new short in the 3 sessions before a report. A Monday trigger with a report after Tuesday's close falls inside that window. Wait for the report to pass, then look for a new trigger.
questions.lesson_line: A report inside 3 sessions is a no. Let it pass, then look for a new trigger.

wrong.No; the stall is too short: Five days is inside the 3 to 10 the card allows. The reason to pass is the report.
wrong.Yes, at half the usual size: Size does not fix a report risk. Smaller is still in.
wrong.Yes, but cover before the report: The rule bars the new entry itself in the 3 sessions before a report. Planning to cover early does not change that.

questions.simple: No. The report comes inside 3 sessions, and we open no new short that close to earnings.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (B22, 3 days against 3 sessions)

questions.q: When does the stop move to breakeven on a Wedge Drop short?
choices: Between 2R and 5R, at first cover
The day after entry, to be safe
Never; a short's stop stays where set
At 1R, once it has paid a bit
questions.answer: Between 2R and 5R, at first cover
questions.why: Between 2R and 5R, and by default at the first cover. A stop may move in your favour. It is never moved wider.
questions.lesson_line: Breakeven comes between 2R and 5R, by default at the first cover.

wrong.The day after entry, to be safe: Too early. Our rule starts at 2R of profit.
wrong.Never; a short's stop stays where set: A stop may move in your favour. Only a wider stop is banned.
wrong.At 1R, once it has paid a bit: Too early. Our rule starts at 2R.

questions.simple: The stop moves to breakeven somewhere between 2R and 5R, and by default at the first cover.

reasons: the breakeven range comes from the card

questions.story: Three weeks after a market low the index is still weak. A stock bounces, stalls three days and closes under both averages at 52.58.
questions.q: What risk does our card name here?
choices: Early in a new bull market
The stall is too long for a drop
The stop is too far
The volume is too light
questions.answer: Early in a new bull market
questions.why: Early in a new bull market. Our card says no short early in a new bull market, in a strongly uptrending stock, or too late in the fall. TraderLion warns the same way. In the real GOOGL case on 2019-01-14, three weeks after the December 2018 low, the short was stopped the next session at 0R. The stock was 7.2% above the entry 20 sessions later.
questions.lesson_line: A few weeks off a market low, the bounce is the trend. Do not short it.

wrong.The stall is too long for a drop: Three days is inside the 3 to 10 the card allows.
wrong.The stop is too far: GOOGL's stop was 2.1% away, inside 3%. The distance was fine; the timing was not.
wrong.The volume is too light: Volume grades the day. The risk the card names is the new bull market.

questions.simple: The card warns against shorting early in a new bull market, because the bounce can keep going.

deeper.trap: The index still looked weak: QQQ was under its 50-day on GOOGL's trigger day. But it was only three weeks after the December 2018 low. A weak-looking market does not make it safe to short early in a new bull market.

reasons: +2 rests on the card's proposed criteria and dated example numbers

questions.q: If the honest stop over the trigger day's high is 5% away, you pull it in to 3% to fit.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. If the stop over the trigger day's high is more than about 3% away, you skip the trade or take the smaller size the rules give. You never pull it in. Stop first. The size comes from the stop.
questions.lesson_line: You never pick a size and back-fit a stop inside the noise.
questions.simple: False. If the honest stop is more than about 3% away, we skip the trade or size down, and we never pull the stop in.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (A3 and A13)

questions.story: Your short sits at 2.7R at Thursday's close. Friday it gaps down and opens at 3.5R.
questions.q: What do you do about the first cover?
choices: Judge it; 3R is not a cover order
Cover a third at the open
Cover the whole position now
Add more; the gap confirms it
questions.answer: Judge it; 3R is not a cover order
questions.why: Judge it. The first cover is a judgment, not a fixed third at 3R. We very rarely sell on day 1 of the buy and usually wait until day 3 at the earliest. A 3.5R open is a reason to look hard, not an order to cover. A gap in your favour is not a place to add. It is full size at one price.
questions.lesson_line: A gap past 3R is not a cover order. Judge the first cover.

wrong.Add more; the gap confirms it: Full size at one price. A gap in your favour is not a place to add.
wrong.Cover the whole position now: Nothing says a gap means covering it all. The first cover is a judgment.
wrong.Cover a third at the open: The first cover is a judgment, not a fixed third at 3R.

questions.simple: Judge it. A gap past 3R is not an automatic cover, and we rarely act on day 1.

reasons: rests on the owner's ruling D-013 (the first sell is a judgment)
the short side mirrors the long side (D47)

questions.story: An 8-day stall 9.6% wide breaks under both averages. The stop over the day's high is 2.4% away.
questions.q: How does our card treat that stall?
choices: Take it, graded down for the stall
Skip it; loose stall is no setup
Skip it; a 2.4% stop is too wide
Take it full grade; tight stop
questions.answer: Take it, graded down for the stall
questions.why: Take it, graded down. Wide, loose action before the drop is graded down, not excluded. The stall here is 9.6% wide over 8 days, and a tight stop does not repair that. DXCM 2022-04-18 was this setup: an 8-day stall 9.6% wide, stopped at 0R by a 124.00 high. The stock then fell hard.
questions.lesson_line: A wide, loose stall grades the trade down. A tight stop does not fix it.

wrong.Skip it; loose stall is no setup: The card grades wide, loose action down, not out. It is still a trade, at a lower grade.
wrong.Skip it; a 2.4% stop is too wide: The stop is inside the 3% line. The wide stall is what grades it down, not the stop.
wrong.Take it full grade; tight stop: A tight stop does not fix a loose stall. The 9.6% wide stall is what grades it down.

questions.simple: It is taken, but graded down, because a wide, loose stall lowers the grade rather than ruling the trade out.

deeper.trap: Do not read a 2.4% stop as proof of quality. DXCM's stop sat inside the 3% line and was still taken at 0R. The stock then fell hard, so the stop was hit and the direction was right.

reasons: rests on a proposed card criterion awaiting owner review
fixed before (cold check)

questions.q: An index closes 5% over its 10-day EMA. By Kell's own note, what is that?
choices: An extension; price is stretched
A healthy trend; nothing to do yet
A Wedge Drop, already confirmed
A Wedge Pop, buy the breakout
questions.answer: An extension; price is stretched
questions.why: An extension; price is stretched. Kell called QQQ a little ahead of itself at 4-5% above its daily 10-day EMA on February 2nd. We use the 9 and 20 EMA. The Wedge Drop came on 2/16 and 2/17. Our card sets about 4% or more over the 9 EMA for an index. The extension is the top. The drop is the close down through the averages days later.
questions.lesson_line: Far above the fast average, the rally is tired. Watch for the stall.

wrong.A healthy trend; nothing to do yet: An index 5% over its 10-day EMA is stretched, not healthy. Kell's note says so.
wrong.A Wedge Drop, already confirmed: The drop is the close back down through the averages, days after the top. A stretched index has not done that yet.
wrong.A Wedge Pop, buy the breakout: A pop is the close up through the averages out of a coil. This index is far above them.

questions.simple: Kell called an index 4 to 5 percent above its 10-day average a little ahead of itself, so 5 percent is stretched.

reasons: a threshold the card proposes (about 4% for an index)
fixed before (cold check)

questions.story: Same stall, two drops. Drop A closes mid-range on light volume. Drop B gaps down, closes at its low, on heavy volume.
questions.q: Which gets the higher grade?
choices: Drop B; sellers were in control
Drop A; quiet is better
Equal; only averages matter
Drop A; more room to fall
questions.answer: Drop B; sellers were in control
questions.why: Drop B, the gap down closing at its low. It is the stronger drop: Kell calls the drop an influx of sellers, and TraderLion adds increased selling pressure. The card wants a wide red bar or a gap down closing near its low, in the lower 40%. A mid-range close is the weaker day. Grading stays a judgment call.
questions.lesson_line: A close at the low, on sellers, grades the day up. A mid-range close grades it down.

wrong.Drop A; quiet is better: Quiet is for the stall. The drop wants sellers.
wrong.Equal; only averages matter: The averages are the trigger. The close in the day's range is part of the grade.
wrong.Drop A; more room to fall: The card wants the close in the lower 40% of the range. A mid-range close is the weaker day.

questions.simple: Drop B, the gap down that closes at its low. It shows sellers in control, and our card wants the close in the lower 40%.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook and a held decision (D-006, trigger volume)

questions.q: Our card prefers a 200-day that is lower than it was 20 sessions ago.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. The card prefers a falling 200-day: lower than it was 20 sessions ago. It is a preference, not a gate. The gate is a close under the 200-day. WHR's August 2002 drop came under a falling 200-day, in a bear market.
questions.lesson_line: Under a falling 200-day the trend is on your side. Prefer it.
questions.simple: True. We prefer a 200-day average that is lower than it was 20 sessions ago, because the bigger trend is down.

reasons: rests on a proposed card criterion awaiting owner review

questions.q: Account 50,000. Risk 1%. Short at 131.23, stop 134.79. How many shares?
questions.answer: 140 shares
questions.why: 140 shares. Risk is 50,000 x 1%. Risk per share is the stop minus the fill: 134.79 - 131.23. Divide the first by the second and round down to 140. The stop sets the size, never the other way round.
questions.lesson_line: Risk sets the size. Divide the dollars you risk by the distance to the stop.
questions.simple: Divide the 1% risk by the distance to the stop, then round down. That gives 140 shares.

reasons: +2 a computed key

choices: 381 shares
184 shares
140 shares
1,404 shares

wrong.381 shares: Divided the account by the price and ignored the stop.
wrong.184 shares: Divided the risk dollars by the stop's percent, not by the dollars per share.
wrong.1,404 shares: Typed the risk as ten times too big, so the share count came out ten times too big.

questions.story: Short from 52.58, stop 53.70. The next session trades up through 53.70 and closes at 54.33.
questions.q: What happened to the trade?
choices: Stopped at 53.70; a planned loss
Still short; the stop needs a close
Covered at the close, 54.33
Stopped; you may re-short at once
questions.answer: Stopped at 53.70; a planned loss
questions.why: Stopped at 53.70, a planned loss. The stop is the exit, and it is never moved wider. The price traded up through 53.70 the next session, so the trade ended there. The close at 54.33 is where you would be with no stop. GOOGL 2019-01-14 did this: stopped on day 1. A new short needs a new trigger.
questions.lesson_line: A close above the trigger day's high means the stop already went. The stop is the exit.

wrong.Still short; the stop needs a close: The stop is an order, not a close you wait for. It filled when the price traded through 53.70.
wrong.Covered at the close, 54.33: The stop went at 53.70 during the day. The close is where you would be if you had no stop.
wrong.Stopped; you may re-short at once: After a stop-out a new short needs a new trigger, as a new trade with its own stop.

questions.simple: The stop at 53.70 was the exit, so the trade ended there as a planned loss, not at the 54.33 close.

deeper.trap: The close at 54.33 is not your exit price. Waiting for a close back under 53.70 turns a planned loss into a larger one. The stop is the exit.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (A4)

questions.story: You are short and have already covered part of it. Now the stock rallies into its falling 9 and 20 EMAs and stalls under them.
questions.q: What is that?
choices: A crossback; hold, trail decides
The setup is failing; cover it now
A place to add to the short
A Wedge Pop; buy the rally
questions.answer: A crossback; hold, trail decides
questions.why: A crossback. Kell: a downside EMA Crossback retests the moving averages and is met with more resistance, pushing the stock lower. A rally that stalls under the falling averages is a place to hold, not to panic. The trail still covers on a close back above the 9 or 20 EMA. It is not a place to add: that would be a new trade with its own stop.
questions.lesson_line: The first rally into the falling averages is expected. Hold it, and let the trail speak.

wrong.The setup is failing; cover it now: Failing is a close back above both averages. A stall under them is the next stage, not a failure.
wrong.A place to add to the short: No adding. One price, one stop; the crossback can be a new trade.
wrong.A Wedge Pop; buy the rally: A pop closes up through both averages. This rally stalled under them.

questions.simple: This is a rally back into the falling averages. Kell expects it to meet resistance, so we hold and let the trail decide.

deeper.trap: A crossback is not a failure. The setup fails on a close back above both averages. Adding at the crossback is the common slip, and Kell's own page offers it. Our rule says no: one price and one stop, and a crossback is a new trade or nothing.

reasons: rests on a proposed card criterion awaiting owner review
tied to a held decision (D-002)

questions.q: The stock is hard to borrow with a high fee. The chart is an A+ Wedge Drop. Your call?
choices: Skip it; the borrow comes first
Skip it; chart is stretched
Short it at half size
Short it; the A+ chart wins
questions.answer: Skip it; the borrow comes first
questions.why: Skip it. We skip a short when the stock is hard to borrow or the borrow fee is high, however good the chart is. The card wants a stock that is easy to borrow at a fair fee. Half size does not help, because the stock fails the rule before size comes up.
questions.lesson_line: A short you cannot borrow cleanly is not a short. Skip it.

wrong.Skip it; chart is stretched: The chart is an A+ Wedge Drop, so it is not the problem. The reason to skip is the borrow.
wrong.Short it at half size: Half of a hard borrow is still a hard borrow. The rule is skip.
wrong.Short it; the A+ chart wins: The borrow comes before the chart. The rule skips a hard-to-borrow short, however good it looks.

questions.simple: Skip it. We pass on any short that is hard to borrow or carries a high fee, even with an A+ chart.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (D48)

questions.q: A blow-off top shorted on its climax day above the 200-day is the Parabolic Short's trade, not a Wedge Drop.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. A short above the 200-day after a blow-off is the Parabolic Short, taken on its climax day with its own checklist. The Wedge Drop comes days later, after a stall within 1 ATR of the 10-day EMA. Bracco's target for the Parabolic Short is the 9-day EMA, which acts as a magnet for mean reversion.
questions.lesson_line: Shorting the blow-off is a different setup. The Wedge Drop comes days later, back at the averages.
questions.simple: True. Shorting a blow-off on its climax day is the Parabolic Short, and a Wedge Drop comes days later.

deeper.counter: Timing separates the two. A Parabolic Short is the climax day of a 3 to 5 day burst, 10% or more over the 9-day EMA. A Wedge Drop needs the stall first, then the close through the averages.

reasons: +2 rests on a held decision (D-040, the parabolic exception)

questions.story: A stock in an uptrend bounces, stalls on its averages and closes under both. The close is 8.3% above its 200-day.
questions.q: What is it for us?
choices: A sell signal for a long, not a short
An A+ short
A Wedge Pop
A parabolic short
questions.answer: A sell signal for a long, not a short
questions.why: A sell signal, not a short. Shorts only below the 200-day. V 2021-05-10 was this, above the 200-day in an uptrend. The short ran 0.93R and was stopped.
questions.lesson_line: Above the 200-day the drop tells a long holder to sell. It gives a short seller nothing.

wrong.An A+ short: No short above the 200-day, however clean the stall. That is a hard rule.
wrong.A Wedge Pop: A pop closes up through the averages. This closed down through them.
wrong.A parabolic short: A parabolic short is a climax day after a 3 to 5 day burst. This is a stall and a drop.

questions.story: In a five-day stall, one close sits 1.6 ATR over the 9 EMA. Then the stock closes under both averages.
questions.q: Does that pass our stall test?
choices: No; one close was past 1 ATR
Yes; five days is enough
Yes; 1.6 ATR is fine
No; five days is too short
questions.answer: No; one close was past 1 ATR
questions.why: No. Through the stall no close is more than 1 ATR from the 9 EMA. One close at 1.6 ATR fails that test. Five days is inside the 3 to 10 the card allows, so length is not the problem. The 1 ATR is the card's proposed number.
questions.lesson_line: Count the quiet days. One close too far from the 9 EMA and it is not a stall.

wrong.Yes; five days is enough: Length is one test. The distance is another, and one close failed it.
wrong.No; five days is too short: Five days is inside the 3 to 10 sessions the card allows.
wrong.Yes; 1.6 ATR is fine: The card says no close is more than 1 ATR from the 9 EMA. This one is past it.

questions.simple: No. One close past 1 ATR from the 9 EMA breaks the stall test, even in a five-day stall.

deeper.trap: One stretched close breaks a stall. A close that far from the 9 EMA means the move is still extended with no real stall, so it is not a Wedge Drop.

reasons: rests on a proposed card criterion awaiting owner review

questions.story: In the stall the up days averaged 2.84 times the volume of the down days. Then a close under both averages.
questions.q: What was the stall?
choices: Accumulation; pass on the short
A clean stall; short it at once
Distribution; sellers are in charge
Accumulation; short with a wide stop
questions.answer: Accumulation; pass on the short
questions.why: Accumulation. A clean stall has the up days on lighter volume than the down days. Here the up days averaged 2.84 times the volume of the down days, which is buyers stepping in. VZ 2010-06-30 did this, and the short was stopped as the stock rallied through the averages.
questions.lesson_line: Heavy up days in the stall mean someone is buying. Do not short them.

wrong.A clean stall; short it at once: The averages were lost, but the volume told the other story. The stall gate fails.
wrong.Distribution; sellers are in charge: Heavy up days mean buyers, not sellers. Distribution is the reverse: heavier selling volume.
wrong.Accumulation; short with a wide stop: A stop never goes wider to fit a trade. The stall's volume gate failed, so we pass.

questions.simple: Heavy volume on the up days means buyers were stepping in, so the stall was accumulation and we pass on the short.

deeper.trap: The close under both averages is only one gate. The stall's volume is another, and here it failed. VZ looked like a Wedge Drop on the chart, ran 0.54R, then was stopped as the stock rallied through the averages.

reasons: rests on a proposed card criterion awaiting owner review

questions.story: The stock is 25% over its 9-day EMA on the fifth straight up day. It gaps up, then closes red.
questions.q: Which setup is that?
choices: The Parabolic Short, climax day
A Wedge Drop, after a quiet stall
A Wedge Pop, out of a tight coil
A downside crossback, a retest
questions.answer: The Parabolic Short, climax day
questions.why: The Parabolic Short. It is shorted on the climax day of a 3 to 5 day burst, 10% or more over the 9-day EMA. Here the stock is 25% over it on the fifth straight up day. A Wedge Drop comes days later, after a stall within 1 ATR of the 9 EMA. Bracco's target for a parabolic short is the 9-day EMA, which acts as a magnet for mean reversion.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the distance to the averages. Far above them on the climax day is the other setup.

wrong.A Wedge Drop, after a quiet stall: No stall on the averages, and price is far above them. The drop comes days later, back at the averages.
wrong.A Wedge Pop, out of a tight coil: A pop is a close up through the averages out of a coil. This is a blow-off far above them.
wrong.A downside crossback, a retest: A crossback is a rally back into the averages after a drop. Nothing has dropped yet.

questions.simple: A stock far above its 9-day average after a short burst is a Parabolic Short, taken on its climax day.

deeper.trap: Distance is the tell. A Wedge Drop stalls within 1 ATR of the 9 EMA. A Parabolic Short sits 10% or more over the 9-day EMA after a burst of 3 to 5 days. The same red close can show up in both, one at the averages and the other far above them.

reasons: rests on a proposed card criterion awaiting owner review
tied to a held decision (D-040)

questions.story: Price just closed through both EMAs. For two weeks before today it had coiled under them. Today it closed up through both.
questions.q: Which is it?
choices: A Wedge Pop, the mirror setup
A Wedge Drop, a sell signal
A downside crossback, a test
An upside crossback, a test
questions.answer: A Wedge Pop, the mirror setup
questions.why: A Wedge Pop. Look at where price sat before the day and which way it closed. A Wedge Pop coils under the 10 and 20-day EMAs and closes up through both. A Wedge Drop stalls on or just above them and closes down through both. Kell adds that the pop is not simply a cross of the averages: price bars and volume matter too.
questions.lesson_line: Same averages, opposite sides. Which side it came from and which way it closed is the whole tell.

wrong.A Wedge Drop, a sell signal: A drop closes down through the averages from on or just above them. This closed up through them from below.
wrong.A downside crossback, a test: A downside crossback is a rally that stalls under falling averages and is met with resistance. This closed up through them.
wrong.An upside crossback, a test: A crossback is a retest of the averages. This is the first close up through both.

questions.simple: Price coiled under both averages and then closed up through them. That is a Wedge Pop and not a drop.

deeper.trap: A close through the averages is not enough to name the setup. Which side price came from decides it. Coiled under and closed up through both is the Pop. Stalled on or above and closed down through both is the Drop. Kell also warns the pop is not simply a cross, since price bars and volume matter.

reasons: tied to a held decision (D-078)

questions.q: An intraday break of the stall low on the 65-minute chart counts only once the daily close confirms it.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. Kell says hourly and 15-minute charts are for timing entries. Our card counts a break of the stall low on the 65-minute chart only once the daily close confirms it. The daily close is the trigger.
questions.lesson_line: The hourly chart can sharpen the entry. The daily close is still the judge.
questions.simple: True. The hourly break can help time the entry, but our card counts it only after the daily close confirms it.

deeper.trap: Shorting inside the stall before the close confirms is a named mistake. An intraday break of the stall low is only a hint until the daily close confirms it. The drop is a one-day event that the next day confirms or cancels.

reasons: rests on a proposed advanced card rule

questions.q: The 9 EMA is 40.00 and the stock opens at 36.40. How far under the average is the open, in percent?
questions.why: 9.0%. The open is under the average by (40.00 - 36.40) / 40.00 x 100 = 9.0%. That is under 10%, so this test does not stop the short at that open. We skip a short more than 10% under its 9 EMA, checked at the open on a gap down.
questions.lesson_line: Check the stretch at the open on a gap down. Past 10% under the 9 EMA, pass.
questions.simple: Take the average minus the open and divide by the average. That is 9.0%, under the 10% line, so this test lets the short through.

deeper.trap: Divide by the average, not by the open. The average is the line the open sits under. Use average minus open, over average.

reasons: +2 a computed key

wrong.9.9%: Divided by the open, not by the average.
wrong.3.6%: Used the dollar gap as if it were the percent.
wrong.0.9%: A decimal slip. The open is far more than one percent under the average.

questions.story: A failed-push top, a three-day stall, a drop on 3.3x volume. You shorted at 24.74, stop 25.26. It never passes 0.34R; on day 8 the stop is hit.
questions.q: Was that loss a mistake?
choices: No; a planned loss, the stop worked
No; you should have covered at 0.34R
Yes; 3.3x volume said stay out
Yes; the stop was far too tight
questions.answer: No; a planned loss, the stop worked
questions.why: No. A stop hit is the plan working. The stop is the exit and is never widened. This one sat 2.1% over the 24.74 fill, inside the 3% a stop usually stays within. The trade peaked at 0.34R and was stopped on day 8. Volume on the drop does not change what a stop-out is.
questions.lesson_line: A loss taken at plan is the system working. You will take this one again.

wrong.Yes; the stop was far too tight: It sat 2.1% over the fill, inside the usual 3%, and it held until day 8.
wrong.No; you should have covered at 0.34R: Nothing in the plan covers at 0.34R. The first cover is a third at 3R, and the stop is the exit.
wrong.Yes; 3.3x volume said stay out: Volume on the drop grades the day. It does not make a stop-out at plan a mistake.

questions.simple: No. A stop hit is the plan working, because the stop is the exit and the loss was the one we planned.

deeper.trap: A loss is not a mistake just because the setup failed. Judge the trade against the plan: stop first, stop respected, never widened. This trade reached only 0.34R before the stop. That is how a stop works, not a breach of the plan.

reasons: +2 rests on a held decision (D-006, trigger volume)
+1 fixed before

questions.story: You held a long. It closed under both averages and you sold. Two sessions later it closes back above both and runs.
questions.q: What do you do?
choices: Nothing; buy only on a new setup
Buy back now; it was a shakeout
Short it; it will fail again
Wait a few days, then buy it back
questions.answer: Nothing; buy only on a new setup
questions.why: Nothing yet. A Wedge Drop reclaimed within a few sessions was a shakeout. Buy again only on a new setup, as a new trade with its own stop. Selling was still right: the drop is the last exit. Kell: once a stock tops, step aside and let the cycle reset before jumping back in.
questions.lesson_line: A shakeout is not a buy signal. The next setup is.

wrong.Buy back now; it was a shakeout: Knowing it was a shakeout is not a trigger. The re-entry needs its own setup and its own stop.
wrong.Short it; it will fail again: It just reclaimed both averages. Shorting a reclaim is fighting strength with no setup.
wrong.Wait a few days, then buy it back: A clock is not a trigger. Buy again only when the setup triggers again, as a new trade with its own stop.

questions.simple: Do nothing yet. A reclaimed drop was a shakeout, but we buy again only on a new setup with its own stop.

deeper.trap: The hindsight trap is feeling that selling was a mistake because it reclaimed and ran. The rule did not change. Selling at the drop was the plan, and getting back in is a new decision with a new stop. Shorting the reclaim is the opposite error, fighting a stock that just took back both averages.

reasons: a card rule built on the settled re-entry rule

questions.story: The stall breaks on a gap down and every other rule checks out. The fill is 90.85 and the stop over the high is 93.53, 3.0% away.
questions.q: Take it?
choices: Yes; the stop fits the 3% line
No; never short a gap down
Yes, but pull the stop to 2%
No; 3.0% is not under 3%
questions.answer: Yes; the stop fits the 3% line
questions.why: Yes. The stop usually sits within about 3% of the fill, and this one sits right at it. Skip or size down only when the stop is more than about 3% away. Never pull it in. TSM 2022-06-09 was this trade: a gap down through the stall low. It reached 6.4R at best, with 3R on day 9.
questions.lesson_line: Right at 3% is inside the line. Past it, size down or skip; never pull it in.

wrong.No; never short a gap down: A gap down closing near its low is a fine trigger day. The question is only the stop's distance.
wrong.Yes, but pull the stop to 2%: Never pull the stop in to fit. It sits over the high or the trade is skipped.
wrong.No; 3.0% is not under 3%: The line is about 3%, and skip applies only when the stop is more than about 3% away. This one is at the line, not past it.

questions.simple: Take it. The stop is about 3 percent away, which is right at the line and not past it.

deeper.trap: The trap is the fix. If the stop were past the line, the answer would be to skip or size down. Never pull the stop in to make it fit. Here nothing needs fixing: the stop sits right at 3.0%, and about 3% is the line.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook

questions.story: Ten sessions after the short, the trade is up 1.4R and drifting sideways on the averages.
questions.q: What does our rule say?
choices: Hold; it is past the 1R bar
Cover; ten sessions is the limit
Cover; it has stopped moving
Add on a pop to the averages
questions.answer: Hold; it is past the 1R bar
questions.why: Hold. The time stop closes a trade still under 1R after 10 trading days. This one is up 1.4R, so the time stop does not apply. The stop, the covers and the trail still run the trade.
questions.lesson_line: Under 1R after ten days, out. Past 1R, the other rules run the trade.

wrong.Cover; ten sessions is the limit: The time stop covers a trade still under 1R after 10 sessions. This one is past 1R.
wrong.Cover; it has stopped moving: Drifting alone is not the rule. Under 1R after 10 sessions is.
wrong.Add on a pop to the averages: No adding. Full size at one price with one stop.

questions.simple: Hold. The time stop is only for a trade still under 1R after 10 sessions, and this one is past 1R.

deeper.trap: Reading the rule as 'ten days and out' is the slip. The bar is 1R of profit, and 1.4R clears it.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook

questions.story: The company reported last night. Today, after a six-day stall on the averages, it gaps down and closes under both, near its low.
questions.q: Does the earnings rule block this short?
choices: No; the reaction day is allowed
Yes; no shorts near earnings
Yes; wait 3 sessions post-report
No; earnings only blocks longs
questions.answer: No; the reaction day is allowed
questions.why: No. The rule is no new short in the 3 sessions BEFORE a report. A Wedge Drop that is the earnings reaction itself is allowed, after the report. The report here came last night, so the sessions before it are over.
questions.lesson_line: Before the report, wait. The reaction day can be the drop.

wrong.Yes; no shorts near earnings: The rule bars new shorts in the 3 sessions before a report. This report is already out.
wrong.Yes; wait 3 sessions post-report: There is no waiting period after a report. The gap through the averages is the trigger.
wrong.No; earnings only blocks longs: The 3-session rule covers new shorts too. It is the report being over that frees this one.

questions.simple: No. The rule only bars new shorts in the 3 sessions before a report, and this drop is the reaction day after it.

deeper.trap: There are two ways to get this wrong. One is shorting in the 3 sessions before the report, which the rule bars. The other is treating the reaction day as blocked too. The rule counts the 3 sessions before a report, not the days after it. The other gates still apply, so the drop still needs its stall and its close under both averages.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook

questions.q: By our card, which RS rating fits a Wedge Drop short?
choices: 20 or less, in a weak group
80 or more, strong group
Any rating; chart decides
50 or less, weak group
questions.answer: 20 or less, in a weak group
questions.why: 20 or less, in a weak group. Shorts are the mirror of buying leaders: the weakest stocks, an RS rating of 20 or less, in the weakest groups. The card asks the same: RS rating 20 or less, in a weak group. In our own words, we are extremely picky with shorts.
questions.lesson_line: Short the weakest in the weakest groups. The mirror of buying leaders.

wrong.80 or more, strong group: That is the leader's side. Shorts are the mirror: the weakest stocks in the weakest groups.
wrong.Any rating; chart decides: The chart is one gate. Weakness is another.
wrong.50 or less, weak group: The line is 20 or less, not 50.

questions.simple: We short the weakest stocks, an RS rating of 20 or less, in the weakest groups. It is the mirror of buying leaders.

deeper.trap: RS of 20 or less is a gate, not a trigger. The stock also needs the 200-day, the market reading, the stall and the close through the averages. We are extremely picky: one or two shorts per cycle.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (C31, the short mirror)

questions.story: The trigger level was 64.63. You missed the close. Next morning the stock opens at 61.50.
questions.q: Short at the open?
choices: No; over 4% under the trigger
Yes; the drop is now confirmed
Yes, at half the usual size
No; never short at the open
questions.answer: No; over 4% under the trigger
questions.why: No. 61.50 is more than 4% under 64.63, and no short goes more than 4% under the trigger level. Chasing costs size: the stop stays over the high, so the distance grows and the shares shrink.
questions.lesson_line: Four percent under the trigger and I am done. The next stall will come.

wrong.Yes; the drop is now confirmed: Confirmed and too far away are both true. The chase line is 4%.
wrong.Yes, at half the usual size: Half of a chased entry is still a chased entry.
wrong.No; never short at the open: The card allows a market order at the next open. The 4% line is what blocks this one.

questions.simple: No. The open is already more than 4 percent under the trigger level, so we do not chase it.

deeper.trap: The 4% line is measured from the trigger level, not from where you wish you had filled. Missing the close does not open a wider window. A later short needs a new stall and a new close under both averages.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook
fixed before (cold check)

questions.story: The reading is Red. A stock under its falling 200-day bounces into its 50-day, makes a lower high, stalls five days and closes under both averages.
questions.q: What is it by our rules?
choices: A candidate; the gates come next
A short now; Red means shorts
A candidate, but Red blocks it
A sell signal for longs, no short
questions.answer: A candidate; the gates come next
questions.why: A short candidate. The reading is Red, which is mostly cash plus shorts below the 200-day. The stock is under a falling 200-day, bounced into the 50-day and made a lower high. That is the top the card grades highest. Our own frame is a decent pop back up, rejected at the 50-day or 20-day EMA. The stall is five days, inside 3 to 10.
questions.lesson_line: Red market, under the 200-day, a pop that fails at the 50-day: a short candidate. Then check the gates.

wrong.A sell signal for longs, no short: Above the 200-day it would be. Under a falling 200-day in a Red market it can be the short.
wrong.A short now; Red means shorts: Red and the 200-day are two gates. The stop, the borrow, the report window and the RS rating still have to pass.
wrong.A candidate, but Red blocks it: Red does not block it. Red is mostly cash, plus shorts below the 200-day, and this stock is under it.

questions.simple: It is a short candidate. The market is Red, the stock is under its 200-day, and the bounce failed at the 50-day.

deeper.trap: A candidate is not a trade yet. The stop must fit within about 3%. The stock must be easy to borrow. No report may fall in the next 3 sessions, and the RS rating should be 20 or less. Fail one, and it is a skip.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook and a held decision (D-023, the market filter)
+1 fixed before

questions.story: GS, August 2011. A bounce dies at the falling 50-day, then a four-day stall. Today it trades down through both averages and the stall low, and closes at 131.23 on 1.2x volume. The day's high is 134.76.
questions.q: Write the plan: entry, stop, first cover day.
choices: Through trigger; stop 134.79; day 3+
Through trigger; stop 134.79; day 1
At the close; stop 134.79; day 3+
Through trigger; stop 133.00; day 3+
questions.answer: Through trigger; stop 134.79; day 3+
questions.why: Short as price trades through the trigger, stop 134.79, first cover on day 3 or later. Shorts enter like buys, never at the close. The stop is a few cents over the day's high of 134.76, about 2.7% from 131.23, inside the 3%. We very rarely sell on day 1 and usually wait until day 3 at the earliest. Measured from the 131.23 close, GS reached 3R on day 4.
questions.lesson_line: Entry, stop, cover, trail. Write it before it triggers; execute it without a debate.

wrong.Through trigger; stop 134.79; day 1: We very rarely sell on day 1 of the buy. The first cover is a judgment, usually day 3 or later.
wrong.At the close; stop 134.79; day 3+: Shorts enter like buys, as price trades through the trigger. Never at the close.
wrong.Through trigger; stop 133.00; day 3+: A stop at 133.00 sits inside the day's range, under the high of 134.76.

questions.simple: Short through the trigger, stop a few cents over the day's high, first cover on day 3 or later.

deeper.example: GS, 2011-08-02: the bounce died at the falling 50-day, then a four-day stall, then a close at 131.23. The stop at 134.79 was about 2.7% away. Measured from that close, 3R came on day 4. At best it reached 13.2R, a high-water mark on a fixed stop, not a result to bank.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook and the D-013 first-sell judgment
the short entry on the close is not covered by D-003

questions.story: Friday the Nasdaq closed under both its EMAs after a stall, the big AI names leading it lower. You hold six longs.
questions.q: What does the index's Wedge Drop tell you?
choices: Cut longs; the market is weak
Buy the dip in the big leaders
Nothing; only single stocks matter
Hold; wait for the 200-day to break
questions.answer: Cut longs; the market is weak
questions.why: Cut long exposure. The index's own Wedge Drop is a reason to cut exposure in any market. It is a warning that the market as a whole is weakening. Kell: ideally any long positions have been closed at the Wedge Drop. Bracco called the Nasdaq's drop the start of another leg down.
questions.lesson_line: When the index wedge drops, your longs are on notice. Reduce first, ask later.

wrong.Buy the dip in the big leaders: Leaders falling through their averages is a sign to get defensive, not to buy.
wrong.Nothing; only single stocks matter: Kell names the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq. The index's drop is the warning for every long.
wrong.Hold; wait for the 200-day to break: The card cuts long exposure on the index's own drop, in any market. It does not wait for the 200-day.

questions.simple: Cut long exposure. An index Wedge Drop warns that the whole market is weakening, whatever your stocks look like.

deeper.trap: Buying the dip treats the drop as a pullback inside a trend. Kell read an index drop as confirmation of a deeper pullback. Waiting for the 200-day treats it as a stock rule. The card cuts on the index's own drop, in any market.

reasons: a card rule, proposed

questions.story: Kell flags a laggard: a loss of 166.50 would trigger a Wedge Drop short. It closes at 166.35, 19% under its 200-day, in a strong market, and he adds it might just be an avoid.
questions.q: Take it?
choices: Pass; the market is too strong
Short; it is under the 200-day
Short; Kell flagged the stock
Pass; a laggard is never shorted
questions.answer: Pass; the market is too strong
questions.why: Pass. The stock is 19% under its 200-day, so that gate is met. The market gate is not: our card bars shorts on a Green or Yellow reading or early in a new bull market, and TraderLion says to avoid shorting early in new bull markets or strong uptrending stocks. Kell hedged his own flag: it might just be an avoid. TSLA 2023-05-15 failed: a 1R loss, then up 55.5% over the next 20 sessions.
questions.lesson_line: Under the 200-day is one gate. A strong market fails another, and the originator's own hedge was the tell.

wrong.Short; it is under the 200-day: The 200-day gate passed. The market gate did not, and the stock rose 55.5% in 20 sessions.
wrong.Short; Kell flagged the stock: He also wrote it might just be an avoid. A flag is not a plan; your own entry, stop and read are.
wrong.Pass; a laggard is never shorted: A laggard is what a short wants: a weak stock. The gate that fails here is the strong market.

questions.simple: Pass. The stock is weak, but the market is strong, and Kell himself said it might just be an avoid.

deeper.trap: Under the 200-day is one gate, not the whole test. TSLA sat 19% under it and still ran 55.5% in 20 sessions. A flag from the originator is a lead, not a plan: Kell wrote that it might just be an avoid on this very name.

reasons: tied to a held decision (D-023)
one dated example carries the proof (d37)

questions.q: Hidden ticker; the trigger day is the last bar. The 200-day is on the chart. On the 200-day test alone, is a short allowed?
choices: Yes; the close is under the 200-day
No; the close is above the 200-day
No; the stall is wide and loose
Yes; a close under the 50-day is enough
questions.answer: Yes; the close is under the 200-day
questions.why: Yes. On the 200-day test alone, a short is allowed because the trigger-day close is under the 200-day. DXCM on 2026-03-05 closed 3.9% under it. The bounce topped where the 50-day meets the flat 200-day, then a seven-day stall. The stop sat right at the 3% limit. It ran 6.7R at best, with 3R on day 6. The other gates still have to pass.
questions.lesson_line: Under the 200-day, a pop that failed at the 50-day, a tight stall: the short is allowed. Then check the rest.

wrong.No; the close is above the 200-day: Look again: the close sits under the 200-day, not above it.
wrong.No; the stall is wide and loose: This question asks about the 200-day test alone. The stall is a different gate, graded elsewhere.
wrong.Yes; a close under the 50-day is enough: The hard line is the 200-day simple moving average. The 50-day is not the test.

questions.simple: Yes. The close is under the 200-day, so a short passes that test, but the other rules still apply.

deeper.example: DXCM, 2026-03-05: short 70.69, stop 72.79, which is 3.0% away. 3R came on day 6 and it reached 6.7R at best. That is a high-water mark on a fixed stop, not a result to bank.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (B26, a hard rule)
+1 fixed before

questions.q: Hidden ticker; the trigger day is the last bar. A clean stall, then a close under both averages, 8.3% above the 200-day. Short or pass?
choices: Pass; it sits above the 200-day
Take it; both averages are lost
Take it, but at half the size
Pass; a stall must run 10 sessions
questions.answer: Pass; it sits above the 200-day
questions.why: Pass. The close is 8.3% above the 200-day, and shorts are only taken below it. Above it the same event is a sell signal for a long in an uptrend, not a short. The short here ran 0.93R and was stopped. Check the 200-day before the averages.
questions.lesson_line: The averages said drop; the 200-day said no short. The 200-day wins.

wrong.Take it; both averages are lost: The close through the averages is the event. The 200-day is the gate, and the close is above it.
wrong.Take it, but at half the size: Size does not fix a failed gate. Above the 200-day this is a sell signal for a long, not a short.
wrong.Pass; a stall must run 10 sessions: The card's stall is 3 to 10 sessions, not a fixed 10. The reason to pass here is the 200-day.

questions.simple: Pass. The close is above the 200-day, so this is a sell signal for a long holder and not a short.

deeper.trap: The averages are the event and the 200-day is the gate. A clean stall and a close under both averages look the same, above the 200-day or under it. One line tells them apart.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook

questions.q: A stop at the top of a wide stall is acceptable when it sits within about 3% of the entry.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. The card's stop is a few cents over the trigger day's high. It is not the top of a wide stall, unless that fits about 3%. A stop more than about 3% away means skip or take the smaller size the rules give. Never pull it in. TraderLion's page asks for tight stops on this short.
questions.lesson_line: The stall top is a level, not the default stop. It works only inside the 3% line.
questions.simple: True. The top of a wide stall works as the stop only when it sits within about 3% of the entry.

deeper.counter: A wide stall is not a ban. The card grades wide, loose action down, not out. But the stop is a separate test. A stall top more than about 3% away fails it, so the trade is skipped or sized down.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook

questions.q: A Wedge Drop usually takes months to form, like the classical rising wedge.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. ChartSchool says the classical rising wedge usually forms over a three to six month period. Our Wedge Drop is a stall of 3 to 10 sessions tight into the moving averages, then one close down through them. They share a name, not a time scale.
questions.lesson_line: Same name, different time scale. Ours is days on the averages, not months of trendlines.
questions.simple: False. The classical rising wedge takes months, while a Wedge Drop is a few days resting on the averages, then one close.

reasons: the stall length is a proposed card number

questions.q: Which market reading means mostly cash, plus shorts?
choices: Red
Orange
Yellow
Green
questions.answer: Red
questions.why: Red. In a Red market we hold mostly cash, plus shorts below the 200-day. Green is full risk, up to 10 positions. Yellow is smaller and fewer. Orange is only A+ setups.
questions.lesson_line: Green is full risk, Yellow smaller, Orange only A+, Red mostly cash and shorts.

wrong.Orange: Orange is only A+ setups, not mostly cash.
wrong.Yellow: Yellow is smaller size and fewer positions.
wrong.Green: Green is full risk and up to 10 positions.

questions.simple: Red is mostly cash, plus shorts below the 200-day. Green is full risk, Yellow smaller and fewer, Orange only A+.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (F65 and D46)

questions.q: Which of these does our card say not to short?
choices: A stock early in a new bull market
A stock under a falling 200-day
A bounce that fails at the 50-day

questions.q: You hold what is left of a short and trail the 9 EMA. Price pokes above it at noon, then closes under it. Cover?
choices: No, the close under it keeps you in
Yes, any trade above it is a cover
Yes, cover half and trail the rest
Yes, a poke shows buyers are back
questions.answer: No, the close under it keeps you in
questions.why: No. The trail is the 9 EMA for a fast mover or the 20 EMA for a steadier one. We cover what is left on a close back above it, not on a touch. Here the stock closed under the line, so the short stays on. A rally that stalls under the falling averages is a place to hold.
questions.lesson_line: Cover on the close back above the line, not on the poke.

wrong.Yes, any trade above it is a cover: A touch is not a close. We cover only on a close back above the trail, so a poke that fades by the close changes nothing.
wrong.Yes, cover half and trail the rest: What is left comes off in one piece on a close back above the line. A poke that fades by the close changes nothing.
wrong.Yes, a poke shows buyers are back: A poke is not buyers taking over. A rally that stalls under the falling averages is a place to hold.
